body.text: On northern Australia’s coastline, communities are exploring how blacklip rock oysters could create businesses and employment. On cattle stations, producers and researchers are testing more resilient farming systems. In remote clinics, eye-screening technology and access to specialists are helping prevent avoidable blindness.

Behind these advances are research partnerships built over nearly a decade through the Cooperative Research Centre for Developing Northern Australia (CRCNA). Preserving and building on that capability requires the federal government to establish and fund a successor before June 2027, with a mandate to connect research, industry and communities across northern Australia.

The Joint Standing Committee on Northern Australia unanimously backed this need in its October 2026 report, Developing the north is not a catchphrase. The report’s sixth recommendation calls for 10 years of funding, through to mid-2037, for a northern-based, northern-led capability supporting research, innovation, extension, knowledge translation and place-based development.

The CRCNA’s federal funding ends in June 2027. Cooperative Research Centres are designed as time-limited programs. Simply extending CRCNA would not provide the enduring mandate or diversified funding model northern Australia needs. However, the challenges facing the north, and the opportunities research can unlock, extend well beyond that date.

So we propose the establishment of a Centre for Northern Australia (CNA): an enduring, northern-based organisation that builds on CRCNA’s networks while expanding its role in coordinating research, investment and adoption across the region. Establishing it before CRCNA’s funding ends will preserve the expertise and trust that make these partnerships work.

We were both born and raised in northern Australia. We understand the distances, seasons and determination required to make things work. Through our work at CRCNA, we have seen how connecting local ambitions with knowledge and expertise opens opportunities that receive little national attention.

Australia’s northern development debate often centres on resources, proximity to Asia and strategic importance. Established and emerging industries also need research to diversify regional economies and sustain communities.

That research must respond to northern realities. Wet-season abundance does not guarantee water when needed, farming systems require adaptation to tropical conditions, and commercial opportunities depend on land tenure, cultural authority, environmental sustainability and market access. Climate change makes this work increasingly urgent.

For First Nations communities with deep connections to their traditional ancestral marine environments, known as Sea Country, aquaculture offers pathways to enterprise and economic independence. Research has helped establish growing systems suited to northern conditions. At Kidman Springs in the Northern Territory, practical agricultural knowledge and contemporary science are helping producers adapt to unpredictable seasons, rising costs and changing markets.

Remote health research has connected local workers with specialist expertise, reducing the need for patients to travel vast distances. For example, eye-screening interventions have helped to prevent permanent blindness. For those patients, research changed their lives.

Established in 2017 with A$75 million in federal funding, the CRCNA has supported more than 100 projects involving 272 partners and generated more than A$155 million in collaborative research activity.

Its achievement extends beyond those figures. Researchers learning from Traditional Owners, producers shaping trials and clinicians adapting technology to remote conditions have built place-based innovation ecosystems that carry knowledge between projects and into practice.

Trust takes time. So does testing an industry through several wet seasons. Neither fits neatly within electoral cycles or short funding programs. Research delivers lasting value when people who live with its results help shape it, with First Nations knowledge and leadership central to that approach.

CRCNA’s research funding was fully committed in 2024. Projects will create valuable findings and tools, but the relationships, coordination and institutional knowledge behind them are harder to preserve. Once dispersed, they cannot simply be recreated through another announcement.

The national Ambitious Australia review, a government publication examining research and development, reinforces the need for a more connected research system. Northern challenges span jurisdictions, industries and portfolios. Solutions require collaboration across them.

The CNA would complement universities, the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation, regional development bodies and First Nations institutions by connecting their expertise across northern jurisdictions. Its mandate includes identifying research gaps, brokering partnerships, coordinating investment and supporting adoption.

Put forward as an independent, not-for-profit organisation, the CNA is proposed to have skills-based governance, strong northern representation and meaningful First Nations participation. Federal funding would provide a foundation for contributions from governments, industry and research partners. Success should mean stronger businesses, healthier communities, better decisions and lasting regional capability.

The strategic case extends beyond research policy. Investment in infrastructure, industry and security depends on the communities, workforces and natural systems sustaining it. Water security, food production, health and environmental management are fundamental to national resilience.
The Australian government should commit to establishing the CNA, agree its mandate and secure foundational funding well before CRCNA concludes in June 2027.

We have watched northerners build industries, test unfamiliar crops and improve remote care with limited resources. We are committed to this work because this is home. The future is already taking shape through the people who live here. Australia’s opportunity is to back their ingenuity with research partnerships that endure.
